rag-q19.testing: multi-hop as the real trigger, the costs of a loop, and adaptive routing as the middle ground.
rag-q19.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "In a fixed pipeline, retrieval happens once, in a set order: rewrite, retrieve, rerank, generate. In agentic RAG, retrieval becomes a tool the model calls in a loop: it decides whether to search, what to search for, which source to use, whether the results are good enough, and when to stop."
3 · Where the fixed pipeline wins "That wins on questions a single retrieval can't answer. Multi-hop questions, where the second search depends on the first answer — 'who manages the team that owns the payments service, and what's their on-call policy?' Multi-source questions that need the document index, a SQL warehouse and a web search. And recovery: if results are poor, reformulate and try again. The costs are real. Latency and tokens become variable and can grow a lot. Behaviour is non-deterministic, so evaluation and debugging get harder — you have to evaluate trajectories, not just answers. And every tool the agent can call adds security surface."
5 · What I'd pick "So I rarely choose between the two outright. The production middle ground is adaptive RAG: a router classifies the query; simple lookups take the fixed, cheap path, and only complex or multi-hop questions enter the loop."
Close "The loop has caps from day one — a maximum number of hops, a token budget, a timeout — and a grader that's allowed to abstain."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Fixed pipeline Agentic RAG
retrieval once, fixed order tool calls in a loop
latency / cost predictable variable
multi-hop, multi-source weak strong
evaluation per stage per trajectory

stages.name: Where agentic RAG wins
stages.html: • Second query depends on the first answer; several data sources; iterative refinement after poor results.

stages.name: Where the fixed pipeline wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the cost of the loop (illustrative trace):

Step Action Tokens in Cumulative latency
1 plan + search("payments service owner") 1,200 1.1 s
2 read results, search("team X on-call policy") 3,800 2.6 s
3 grade results, answer 5,200 4.3 s
fixed path, single retrieval answer 2,500 1.4 s

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: does the question need more than one dependent retrieval?
stages.html: • Measure the share of such questions in real traffic; that share is how much of the system should be agentic.

stages.name: What I'd pick

followUps.question: 🧪 Each hop succeeds 90% of the time. What's the success rate of a 4-hop chain?
followUps.html:
About 66%.

0.9⁴ ≈ 0.66

Errors compound across hops. That's why caps, graders and trajectory evaluation matter, and why short chains are preferred.

followUps.question: "Agentic RAG is strictly better."
followUps.html:
No. For single-hop lookups it's slower, costlier and less predictable, with no quality gain.

Question Use
Single-hop lookup the fixed pipeline
Multi-hop or multi-source the agent loop

followUps.question: How do you evaluate an agentic retriever?
followUps.html:
Final-answer correctness plus trajectory metrics.

Trajectory metric
Hops taken
Redundant searches
Whether the right sources were used
Cost and latency per question
Consistency across repeated runs

followUps.question: How does the router decide?
followUps.html:
By labelling query complexity.

Router:small classifier or an LLM calllabel: lookup / multi-hop / aggregationroute

It's trained or prompted with examples from real traffic, and misroutes are logged and reviewed.

followUps.question: What security concerns does the loop add?
followUps.html:
Injection can steer it: the agent reads untrusted text and can call tools.

Control
Tools read-only
Scope the user's permissions
Side effects require approval

Q37 covers the attack.

rag-q20.testing: relational and global questions as the real use cases, and honest build/update costs.
rag-q20.trap: proposing graph-first on a daily-changing corpus.
rag-q20.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Vector RAG finds chunks similar to the question. It has two blind spots. It can't traverse relations: 'which suppliers of the parts used in product X had quality incidents?' requires following links across documents, and no single chunk contains the answer. And it can't answer global questions: 'what are the main themes in these 5,000 customer complaints?' — the answer is spread across everything, so top-k similarity returns an arbitrary handful."
3 · Where vector RAG wins "GraphRAG addresses both. At ingestion, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from every chunk into a knowledge graph. For relational questions, you find the entities in the query and traverse the graph. For global questions, Microsoft's GraphRAG clusters the graph into communities and pre-writes summaries for each, then answers by map-reducing over those summaries. The costs: an LLM extraction pass over the whole corpus, which is expensive; entity resolution — making sure 'J. Smith' and 'John Smith' become one node; a second store to operate; and updates that can rewire the graph and require re-summarising communities rather than just appending."
5 · What I'd pick "The practical middle ground is hybrid: vector search finds entry points, and the graph expands one or two hops around them."
Close "For a corpus that changes daily and mostly gets lookup questions, plain vector plus hybrid search is the better choice."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Question type Vector RAG GraphRAG
"what does policy X say?" overkill
relational / multi-hop weak traversal
global themes across corpus weak (arbitrary top-k) community summaries
frequently changing corpus cheap upserts expensive re-extraction

stages.name: Where GraphRAG wins
stages.html: • Supply chains, org structures, investigations, compliance mapping; "what themes / what connects X and Y".

stages.name: Where vector RAG wins
stages.html:
Prove it — ingestion cost (illustrative):

Corpus: 100k chunks × ~600 tokens
Graph extraction: 1 LLM call per chunk (+ prompt ~1,000 tokens) → ~160M input tokens, plus output
Community summaries: one pass per community at each level after extraction
Vector index: 100k embedding calls, cheap; updates are per-chunk upserts

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: what share of real questions is relational or global?
stages.html: • Classify a sample of real queries. If it's a small share, route only those to a graph path, or skip GraphRAG.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html: • Vector + BM25 for lookups; a scoped graph over the entity types the relational questions need; vector hits as entry points, 1–2 hop expansion; global-summary mode only where themes are asked.

followUps.question: 🧪 "Summarise the main complaint themes across 5,000 tickets." Why does top-10 vector retrieval fail?
followUps.html:
Because it returns the 10 tickets most similar to the question's wording, not a representative sample.

Themes present in thousands of tickets may be missing. The answer needs aggregation across the corpus:

  • Community summaries.
  • Clustering.
  • Map-reduce over all tickets.

followUps.question: "GraphRAG is the next step up from RAG, so we should adopt it."
followUps.html:
It's a different tool, not the next step up.

GraphRAG
Good for relational and global questions
Costs heavy build and update
On lookup-heavy traffic cost without quality gains

followUps.question: What's the hardest part of building the graph?
followUps.html:
Entity resolution and schema.

Task Means
Entity resolution merging variant names into one node
Schema deciding which entity and relation types exist

Errors there propagate into every traversal (Q46).

followUps.question: How do updates work?
followUps.html:
A new document can change more than it adds.

Ripple:new entities and edgesdifferent mergesdifferent communitiessummaries recomputed for the affected communities

Incremental pipelines exist, but they're more complex than vector upserts.

followUps.question: How would you pilot it?
followUps.html:
Small, on the question class that fails today.

Pilot:pick the failing relational question classbuild a graph over only the entity types it needscompare with hybrid vector RAG on those questionsdecide

Compare both answer quality and cost.

dontSay: Graph-first for a daily-changing FAQ corpus.

rag-q21.testing: that recursive splitting is a strong baseline, structure beats both, and semantic must earn its cost.
rag-q21.trap: assuming semantic chunking is strictly better.
rag-q21.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Recursive splitting cuts on a hierarchy of separators — paragraphs, then sentences, then characters — until chunks fit a size limit. It's cheap, deterministic and respects natural boundaries most of the time, which makes it a strong baseline. Semantic chunking embeds each sentence and starts a new chunk where the similarity between consecutive sentences drops, so boundaries follow topic shifts. That can give cleaner chunks for long unstructured text like transcripts, but it costs an embedding pass per sentence at ingestion, adds parameters to tune, and produces uneven chunk sizes."
3 · Where semantic chunking wins "The option that usually beats both is structure-aware chunking when the document has real structure: headings, sections, clauses, list items, tables. The author already marked the topic boundaries; use them. Published comparisons are mixed — semantic chunking doesn't consistently beat a well-configured recursive splitter — so I don't pay for it by default."
Close "I'd measure recall@k and answer quality on the golden set for recursive versus semantic, on the document types where boundaries seem to be the problem."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Recursive Semantic Structure-aware
cost ~free embed every sentence parser quality
determinism high depends on model + threshold high
chunk sizes even uneven follows document
best for general text long unstructured prose, transcripts manuals, contracts, reports

stages.name: Where recursive splitting wins
stages.html: • Mixed corpora, frequent re-ingestion, limited ingest budget.

stages.name: Where semantic chunking wins
stages.html:
• Meeting transcripts, chat logs, long essays without headings.

Prove it — the comparison to run (cells to measure):

Chunker recall@10 faithfulness ingest cost / 1k docs
recursive 400 tokens measure measure measure
semantic (threshold p95 drop) measure measure measure
structure-aware (headings) measure measure measure

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: does the document already mark its topics?
stages.html: • Yes → structure-aware. No, and eval shows boundary failures → try semantic. Otherwise → recursive.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: structure first, recursive fallback, semantic by evidence
stages.html: • Per document type: parser-driven structure for structured docs, recursive elsewhere, semantic only for types where it wins on the golden set.

followUps.question: 🧪 A 1-hour meeting transcript has no headings. Which chunker would you try first?
followUps.html:
Recursive splitting on speaker turns, as the baseline.

Order:recursive, with speaker-turn boundaries as separatorsthen semantic chunking to catch topic shiftscompare on questions about that meeting

Speaker turns are cheap structure worth using.

followUps.question: "Semantic chunking is the modern best practice."
followUps.html:
A candidate to test, not a default.

  • Evidence: mixed.
  • Cost: more compute, and more tuning.

followUps.question: How does semantic chunking pick boundaries?
followUps.html:
Where consecutive sentences stop resembling each other.

Method:embed each sentencecosine distance between neighbourssplit where the distance exceeds a thresholdenforce min and max sizes

The threshold is often a percentile of all the distances.

followUps.question: What does structure-aware chunking need?
followUps.html:
A parser that keeps the structure.

Path:layout-aware PDF parsingMarkdown or HTML with headings, lists and tablessplit on those elementssection path stored as metadata

followUps.question: How would you roll out a chunking change?
followUps.html:
As a parallel index, with everything else frozen.

Rollout:build the parallel indexcompare on the golden set (recall first, then end-to-end)cut over with a version bumpkeep the old index for rollback

Q61 has the evaluation.

dontSay: Changing chunkers without a parallel index and eval.

rag-q22.testing: your-data evaluation over leaderboards, and the axes that matter operationally.
rag-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "On my data, not a leaderboard. MTEB is a useful shortlist, but it averages many tasks and domains, some models are tuned toward it, and it doesn't include my documents or my users' questions."
3 · Baseline process "The process: build a golden set of real queries with their answering chunks — a few hundred is enough to start. Shortlist three to five models across price and hosting options. Embed the corpus with each, using each model's documented query and document prefixes, and measure recall@10 and MRR, sliced by query type and language."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Then weigh the operational axes. Dimension: it drives storage and RAM — 3,072 dimensions costs four times 768. Maximum input length versus my chunk size. Whether it's trained for asymmetric retrieval. Languages. Hosting: API with data leaving the network, or self-hosted with a GPU to run. Cost per million tokens and latency for query embedding."
4 · Deep-dive "Two tools reduce the dimension cost: Matryoshka-trained models let you truncate vectors — search with 256 dimensions, rerank with full — and int8 or binary quantisation shrinks memory with a small recall loss."
6 · Evolve "And treat the choice as versioned: switching models means re-embedding everything, so it's a planned migration, not a config change."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Languages and scripts; domain vocabulary; data residency; corpus size and query QPS.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Prove it — memory per 10M chunks (float32):

3,072 dims × 4 B × 10M = 122.9 GB
1,024 dims × 4 B × 10M =  41.0 GB
  768 dims × 4 B × 10M =  30.7 GB
Matryoshka 256 dims    =  10.2 GB  (search), full dims kept on disk for rescoring
int8 of 1,024 dims     =  10.2 GB

stages.name: Baseline process
stages.html:
Model recall@10 MRR dims max tokens hosting cost / 1M tokens
candidate A measure measure
candidate B measure measure
candidate C measure measure

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Lever Detail
Asymmetry use each model's query and document prefixes exactly (Q5)
Fine-tuning if no model is good enough, fine-tune an open model on domain query–chunk pairs, mined from logs or synthetic
After either measure again

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Silent truncation past max length; mixing model versions in one index; missing prefixes; choosing a multilingual-weak model for non-English users.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html: • Version-stamp vectors; blue/green re-index for model changes (Q31); re-run the golden set on every candidate.

followUps.question: 🧪 Model A: recall@10 0.82, 3,072 dims. Model B: 0.80, 768 dims. 20M chunks. Which?
followUps.html:
B, unless the 2-point gap is significant and matters.

A: 20M × 3,072 dims × 4 bytes ≈ 246 GB
B: 20M ×   768 dims × 4 bytes ≈  61 GB

A reranker can usually recover more than 2 points. First check whether the gap is within noise on the golden set.

followUps.question: "Pick the top MTEB model."
followUps.html:
Shortlist from the leaderboard; decide on your golden set.

A leaderboard average
Isn't your domain or your queries
Top models are often large and costly

followUps.question: What are Matryoshka embeddings?
followUps.html:
Models trained so the first N dimensions are themselves a good embedding.

Use:truncate to 256 dimensions for cheap searchrescore the shortlist with the full vector

A little recall traded for large memory savings.

followUps.question: When would you fine-tune an embedding model?
followUps.html:
When off-the-shelf recall is the bottleneck and the domain differs from general text.

Need
Signal domain vocabulary or relevance differs; recall is the bottleneck
Data a few thousand query–positive pairs, with hard negatives

Often the highest-ROI fine-tune in a RAG stack.

followUps.question: API or self-hosted?
followUps.html:
API when data policy allows and speed matters; self-hosted for control.

API Self-hosted
Gets you speed, no GPU operations residency, lower cost at high volume, fine-tuning
Version control the vendor can deprecate a model and force a re-index on their schedule yours

dontSay: Swapping models without a re-index plan.

rag-q23.testing: that hybrid has costs and must be measured, and knowing the inverse case.
rag-q23.trap: adding hybrid reflexively because it's "best practice".
rag-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Hybrid search isn't free: two indexes, two ingestion paths to keep in sync, a fusion step, and two retrievals per query, which adds latency and operational load."
2 · Where dense-only is enough "It's often not worth it on clean natural-language corpora where questions are conversational and the text has few identifiers: help articles, policies written in prose, general knowledge. A good dense model plus a reranker frequently matches hybrid there, and the second index adds cost without gain."
3 · Where hybrid is mandatory "The inverse case is where hybrid is close to mandatory: corpora full of exact tokens — product codes, part numbers, error messages, ticket IDs, legal citations, drug names — and users who search with them. Dense models blur those strings; BM25 matches them exactly. For some of those corpora, keyword search should even come first. So I decide with a measurement: recall@k for dense-only versus hybrid on the golden set, sliced by query type — identifier queries versus natural-language ones."
Close "If hybrid only helps a small slice, I can route those queries to BM25 rather than running both for everything."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: recall gain vs a second system
stages.html: "Hybrid buys exact-match recall at the cost of a second index, a fusion step and extra latency."

stages.name: Where dense-only is enough
stages.html: • Help centres, narrative policies, general Q&A where users rarely type codes.

stages.name: Where hybrid is mandatory
stages.html:
Prove it — the sliced measurement (cells to measure):

Query slice share of traffic dense recall@10 hybrid recall@10
natural-language questions measure measure measure
contains an ID / code / error string measure measure measure
rare names / new jargon measure measure measure

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: do users search with exact strings?
stages.html: • Mine query logs for tokens matching ID patterns, codes and quoted strings; that share plus the recall gap on it decides.

stages.name: What I'd do
stages.html:
Measured result Do
Big gain on a big slice hybrid with RRF for all traffic
Big gain on a small slice route that slice to BM25
No gain dense + reranker only

followUps.question: 🧪 A user searches "ERR_CONN_RESET 0x80072efd". Predict dense-only behaviour.
followUps.html:
General network-error articles, not the page with that code.

Retriever Result
Dense the code splits into odd tokens with little semantic weight
BM25 finds the page containing that exact string

This is the classic hybrid case.

followUps.question: "Hybrid is best practice, always add it."
followUps.html:
A good default when you haven't measured, not a rule.

On clean prose corpora it can add cost with no gain. Measure the slices:

Slice Hybrid
ID-heavy queries pays
Clean natural-language prose may not

followUps.question: What about learned sparse models like SPLADE?
followUps.html:
Sparse vectors with learned term expansion.

SPLADE-style models
On natural language often better than BM25
Exact terms strengths kept
Operations still a second index to run

followUps.question: Can routing replace hybrid?
followUps.html:
Yes, if identifier queries are detectable.

Router:regex on patterns, or a classifieridentifier queries to BM25everything else to dense

Misroutes need monitoring.

followUps.question: What does hybrid cost operationally?
followUps.html:
Roughly double the retrieval work, plus a second system to keep in step.

Cost
Consistency two indexes updated on every upsert and delete
BM25 configuration analysers and tokenizers: languages, stemming
Fusion logic to build and maintain
Per query about twice the retrieval work

Worth it only where it measurably pays.

rag-q24.testing: matching the transformation to the query's problem, and counting the cost.
rag-q24.trap: decomposing a single-intent query and multiplying cost.
rag-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Each fixes a different query problem, so I match them to the problem."
2 · Where rewriting wins "Rewriting fixes a bad query: vague, misspelled, or conversational — 'what about the premium one?' only makes sense with the chat history. An LLM rewrites it into one standalone, specific query. One extra call, one retrieval."
3 · Where multi-query wins "Multi-query fixes phrasing risk for a single intent: the user's wording might not match the documents' wording, so the LLM writes three to five paraphrases, retrieves for each, and fuses the results with RRF. It's recall insurance. One LLM call, several retrievals."
4 · Where decomposition wins "Decomposition fixes a genuinely multi-part question: 'compare our refund policy for EU and US customers' becomes two sub-questions, each retrieved and answered, then combined. It costs a retrieval per part and sometimes a generation per part. And step-back prompting fixes an over-specific query by also retrieving for the more general question — the principle behind the specific case."
5 · What I'd do "All of them add latency, so I route: conversational follow-ups get rewriting; short or ambiguous queries get multi-query; questions with 'and', 'compare' or several entities get decomposition; everything else goes straight through."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Problem Technique Cost
vague / conversational / misspelled rewrite 1 LLM call, 1 retrieval
wording mismatch risk multi-query + RRF 1 LLM call, N retrievals
several questions in one decomposition 1 LLM call, N retrievals (+ N generations)
too specific step-back 1 LLM call, 2 retrievals

stages.name: Where rewriting wins
stages.html:
History: "What's the price of the Pro plan?"   User: "and the premium one?"
Rewrite: "What is the price of the Premium plan?"

stages.name: Where multi-query wins
stages.html: • Short queries, jargon mismatch, recall-critical domains.

stages.name: Where decomposition wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the cost of transformations per query (illustrative):

Plain:          0 LLM calls · 1 retrieval  · ~60 ms
Rewrite:        1 LLM call  · 1 retrieval  · +300 ms
Multi-query ×4: 1 LLM call  · 4 retrievals · +350 ms
Decompose ×3:   1 LLM call  · 3 retrievals · +300 ms (+ 3 partial answers if map-reduce)

stages.name: What I'd do
stages.claim: route by query type, measure each
stages.html: • A lightweight classifier chooses the transformation; each is evaluated on its slice of the golden set; timeouts fall back to the plain query.

followUps.question: 🧪 "What's the refund window?" gets decomposed into 3 sub-questions. What happens?
followUps.html:
Triple the work, and possibly a worse answer.

Effect
Retrievals and latency ×3
Noise from off-target sub-questions
Answer possibly worse

It's a single-intent query: at most a rewrite.

followUps.question: "Always rewrite queries with an LLM."
followUps.html:
No. Rewrite when there's a reason.

Query Do
Conversational or vague rewrite
Clear pass through

Rewriting adds latency and can drift from the user's intent.

followUps.question: How do you fuse multi-query results?
followUps.html:
Fuse the rankings, then rerank against the original question.

Path:per-query rankingsRRFfused poolrerank against the original question

followUps.question: How do you know if the rewrite hurt?
followUps.html:
Log both versions and compare.

  • Log original and rewritten queries.
  • Compare retrieval metrics on the golden set with and without rewriting.
  • Sample for intent drift.

followUps.question: How does this interact with agentic RAG?
followUps.html:
An agent does these moves dynamically; a fixed router captures most of the value at predictable cost.

Fixed router with transformations Agent loop
Moves chosen up front reformulate, split, retry as it goes
Cost predictable variable
Use for most traffic truly dependent multi-hop questions (Q19)

rag-q25.testing: the problem each pattern solves, and the shared idea of conditional retrieval.
rag-q25.trap: listing names without the problem each solves.
rag-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "All three make retrieval conditional instead of a fixed first step, and each answers a different question."
2 · Mechanism "Self-RAG, from Asai and colleagues in 2023, asks: should I retrieve at all, and is my output supported? The model is trained to emit reflection tokens — retrieve or not, is this passage relevant, is my statement supported, is the answer useful — so it retrieves on demand and critiques its own generation. It needs a specially trained model."
3 · Where it breaks "Corrective RAG, CRAG, asks: are these retrieved documents any good? A lightweight evaluator grades the retrieved set; if it's confident they're relevant, it refines them; if they're poor, it falls back — rewriting the query or searching the web; if ambiguous, it combines both."
4 · How I'd use it "FLARE, forward-looking active retrieval, asks: do I need more information right now? While generating, if the model's next sentence has low-confidence tokens, it uses that tentative sentence as a query, retrieves, and regenerates it. It's aimed at long-form answers where needs emerge mid-way."
5 · Adjacent concept "In production I use the ideas more than the exact papers: a relevance grader on retrieved chunks with a fallback path and an abstention option is the CRAG idea and is cheap and effective."
Close "They all add latency and non-determinism, so they need caps."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: three places to make retrieval conditional
stages.html:
Pattern Question it answers Mechanism
Self-RAG retrieve? is my output supported? trained reflection tokens
CRAG are these documents good? retrieval evaluator + fallback (rewrite / web)
FLARE do I need more info now? low-confidence tokens trigger mid-generation retrieval

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.claim: where each sits in the flow
stages.html:
One loop, three checks:queryretrievegenerateanswer

Each check has a "no" path: Self-RAG skips retrieval, CRAG sends poor documents to a rewrite or a web search before generating, and FLARE goes back to retrieve when the next sentence is low-confidence.

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.claim: model support, latency and fallback risk
stages.html:
• Self-RAG needs a fine-tuned model — not an option with most hosted APIs.
  • FLARE needs token probabilities and repeated generation — latency and API support.
  • CRAG's grader can be wrong; web fallback brings untrusted content.

Prove it — the eval for a CRAG-style grader (cells to measure):

Setup answer correctness abstention on unanswerable p95 added
no grader measure measure 0
grader + abstain measure measure measure
grader + rewrite fallback measure measure measure

stages.name: How I'd use it
stages.claim: a grader with a fallback and caps
stages.html: • Cheap cross-encoder or small-LLM grader on the reranked set; if below threshold, one rewrite-and-retry; if still below, abstain with a helpful message (Q43).

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • These are structured, bounded versions of what an agent loop does freely (Q19).

followUps.question: 🧪 Your grader rejects all retrieved chunks for 12% of queries. What should happen for those?
followUps.html:
One fallback attempt, then abstain.

Path:grader rejects all chunksone fallback (rewrite, or an alternate source)abstain with the reason and a nearer question

Never a forced answer from weak context. Also inspect the 12%: coverage gaps in the corpus are a content problem to fix.

followUps.question: "We use Self-RAG" with a hosted API model.
followUps.html:
Then it isn't Self-RAG, and I'd say so.

Self-RAG With an API model
Needs a model trained to emit reflection tokens —
What you can do — imitate parts with prompts and graders: a different system

followUps.question: Why not always retrieve?
followUps.html:
Because some turns don't need it.

Turn Retrieval
Chit-chat, formatting adds latency for nothing
Answerable from the conversation can inject irrelevant context

Conditional retrieval avoids both.

followUps.question: What does web fallback add as risk?
followUps.html:
Untrusted content and inconsistent sources.

Risk Control
Injection sanitise
Freshness, licensing restrict the domains
Inconsistent sources cite clearly as external

followUps.question: Which would you ship first?
followUps.html:
The CRAG-style grader with abstention.

Why it's first
Cost cheapest
Model support works with any model
Effect directly reduces confidently wrong answers

The others only with clear evidence and model support.

dontSay: A list of names with no problems.
Self-RAG on an unmodified API model.

rag-q26.testing: that retrieval k and generation k are different numbers, each set from data.
rag-q26.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "There are two different ks, and I set them separately."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Retrieval k is how many candidates I pull before reranking. I set it from the golden set: plot recall@k as k grows, and pick the point where it plateaus — often somewhere between 20 and 100. Retrieving more beyond that adds rerank cost without finding more evidence. Generation k is how many chunks go into the prompt. That's bounded by the context budget, by cost per token, and by the fact that models use long contexts unevenly, so more chunks can make answers worse. With a good reranker, three to eight chunks is typical, and I tune it on end-to-end faithfulness and correctness."
3 · Baseline method "The reranker is what lets the second number be small: retrieve wide for recall, rerank, send the few that survive."
4 · Deep-dive "Some refinements: a relevance threshold after reranking instead of a fixed count, so easy questions send two chunks and broad ones send eight; and token-based budgets rather than chunk counts when chunk sizes vary."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Retrieval k (candidate pool) vs generation k (chunks in the prompt).

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Context budget for evidence: 4,000 tokens
Chunk ≈ 400 tokens → generation k ≤ 10, and fewer is usually better
Rerank latency ≈ linear in retrieval k → cap it at the recall plateau

stages.name: Baseline method
stages.html:
Prove it — recall@k from the gold chunk's rank on 20 golden queries:

ranks = [1, 3, 2, 8, 1, 14, 5, 2, 31, 4, 1, 6, 9, 2, 55, 3, 1, 7, 12, 2]   # rank of the gold chunk, 20 golden queries
for k in (1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 50):
    print(k, sum(r <= k for r in ranks) / len(ranks))
# → 1 0.2
# → 3 0.5
# → 5 0.6
# → 10 0.8
# → 20 0.9
# → 50 0.95

Recall keeps rising to k = 50 here, so retrieval k ≈ 50 feeds the reranker; the reranker then decides the 3–5 that reach the prompt.

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html: • Keep chunks whose rerank score passes a calibrated threshold, with a min (1–2) and max (8) — adapts to easy vs broad questions.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: one k for both stages, or k as a quality fix
stages.html:
Failure What goes wrong
One k for both stages retrieval and generation need different numbers
Raising generation k to "fix" wrong answers adds noise and lost-in-the-middle
A huge retrieval k rerank latency blows up

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: re-derive k when any component changes
stages.html: • Re-derive both ks whenever the embedder, chunker or reranker changes; per-query-type ks if slices differ a lot.

followUps.question: 🧪 Answers got worse after raising generation k from 5 to 15. Why?
followUps.html:
Dilution, position and conflict.

Cause Fix
More low-relevance chunks dilute the context reduce k, rerank
The best chunks sit mid-window and are under-used place them at the edges
Conflicting chunks appear fewer, better chunks

followUps.question: "k = 5 is standard."
followUps.html:
There's no standard.

k depends on
Chunk size
Reranker quality
The questions

Derive it from recall curves and end-to-end evals.

followUps.question: Why not send everything the reranker scores highly?
followUps.html:
Because cost grows with every chunk while quality peaks early.

  • Cost: tokens and latency grow with each chunk.
  • Quality: often peaks at a few high-precision chunks.
  • So: cap by tokens.

followUps.question: How does MMR interact with k?
followUps.html:
MMR decides which k to send.

How:it penalises redundancynear-duplicate top chunks are replaced by different ones

Useful when the top chunks are near-duplicates (Q13).

followUps.question: Would you vary k per query?
followUps.html:
Yes, measured on each slice.

Mechanism Example
Rerank-score threshold send what clears it
Query type lookups need 1–3, comparisons need more

dontSay: Raising k to fix wrong answers.
A number without a recall curve.

rag-q27.testing: computation vs description, and the safety controls text-to-SQL needs.
rag-q27.trap: vector-RAG-ing a table and hallucinating totals.
rag-q27.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "The question to ask is whether the answer requires computation over rows or a description of content."
2 · Where text-to-SQL wins "Aggregations, filters, counts, rankings and joins — 'total refunds by region last quarter' — need SQL. Vector retrieval returns a handful of similar rows or chunks; the model then 'sums' whatever it happened to get, which produces confident, wrong totals. Vectors can answer about rows, never over rows."
3 · Where vector RAG wins "Text-to-SQL has its own risks. The model can pick the wrong table or join, misunderstand a column, or produce a query that runs but answers a different question — wrong results are worse than errors. And generated SQL is untrusted code."
4 · The deciding question "So I use controls: expose curated views with clear names and descriptions rather than the raw schema; a read-only role with row limits and timeouts; validate the SQL — only SELECT, only allowed tables — before running; include a few example question-and-SQL pairs; and show the generated SQL or a plain-language explanation of it so users can check it. A semantic layer with defined metrics helps a lot."
5 · What I'd build "Vector RAG fits text in or about the data: product descriptions, support notes, documentation of what a metric means."
Close "Many real questions need both, so a router sends each question — or each part of it — to the right path and merges the results."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: compute over rows vs find text about them
stages.html:
Question Path
"How many enterprise customers churned in Q2?" SQL
"Why do enterprise customers say they churn?" vector RAG over notes/tickets
"Which region had most refunds, and what reasons did customers give?" SQL, then RAG, merged

stages.name: Where text-to-SQL wins
stages.html: • Sums, counts, averages, top-N, joins, time windows; results are exact and reproducible.

stages.name: Where vector RAG wins
stages.html:
Prove it — why vector retrieval can't total a table:

Table: 10,000 refund rows. Question: "total refunds in EMEA last quarter"
Vector RAG: retrieves top-5 similar rows → model sums 5 rows → confidently wrong total
SQL: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM refunds_v WHERE region='EMEA' AND quarter='2026Q2'; → exact

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html: • Yes → SQL with guards. No, it needs explanation or narrative → RAG. Both → decompose and route.

stages.name: What I'd build
stages.claim: a router, guarded SQL, and RAG
stages.html:
Control Why
curated views + column descriptions fewer wrong joins
read-only role, row cap, timeout blast radius
SQL validation (SELECT-only, allow-listed tables) model output is untrusted
examples + semantic layer for metrics consistent definitions
show SQL / explanation user can verify
eval set of question → expected result catches wrong-but-valid SQL

followUps.question: The generated SQL runs and returns a number, but uses orders.created_at instead of orders.shipped_at. How do you catch that?
followUps.html:
Not by running it: execution success says nothing about correctness.

Guard
Evaluation questions with known answers
Definitions clear column descriptions, or a semantic layer that defines "shipped revenue"
Transparency show users the SQL or an explanation

followUps.question: "Just embed the table rows and use RAG."
followUps.html:
Aggregates over a few retrieved rows are wrong.

Need Tool
A few similar rows retrieval
A sum, a count, an average SQL

followUps.question: How do you handle a huge schema?
followUps.html:
Retrieve the schema first.

Path:schema RAG over table and column descriptionsthe relevant tables and columnsgenerate SQL with only those in context

followUps.question: What about SQL injection?
followUps.html:
The model's SQL is untrusted input.

Control
Credentials read-only
Queries validation and allow-lists
User input never string-concatenated into queries run with elevated permissions
Multi-tenant data row-level security

followUps.question: Would you let executives use this unsupervised?
followUps.html:
Only on certified views and metric definitions.

  • Show: the SQL or an explanation, with confidence cues.
  • Offer: a path to an analyst.
  • Why: wrong numbers in an executive decision are costly; that's what the semantic layer and the evals are for.

dontSay: Running generated SQL with write access.

rag-q28.testing: the ANN–filter interaction, and that isolation is an indexing decision.
rag-q28.trap: treating the filter as a query concern.
rag-q28.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "The interaction between approximate nearest-neighbour search and the filter breaks first."
2 · Rule out the fakes "With post-filtering, the index finds the top 100 nearest vectors across all 50 million, then you discard those that aren't this tenant and this date range. If the tenant owns a small fraction of the corpus, almost nothing survives: you get two results, or zero, even though the tenant has perfectly relevant documents. Raising k helps a little and costs a lot. With pre-filtering, you restrict to the tenant's documents first. That's correct, but a graph index like HNSW assumes it can walk through neighbours; when most nodes are excluded, the graph falls apart into disconnected pieces and search either misses results or degrades to a brute-force scan, which is slow for large tenants."
4 · Fix by design "What you want is filtered ANN — the filter evaluated during traversal, with the engine adapting, for example switching to exact search when the filter is very selective. That's the capability to check in any vector store, with a benchmark at your real selectivity. The other design is to make the filter an index choice: partition by tenant — a namespace or shard per tenant, or per group of small tenants — so each query searches a small, dense index. Date filters are then handled with time partitions or with filtered search inside the tenant partition. And since the tenant filter is a security boundary, it must come from the authenticated identity and be tested."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "Selective filters break approximate search: post-filtering starves results, pre-filtering breaks graph navigation."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: is it the filter, or the data?
stages.html:
Test Verdict
Same query without the filter is good; with it, few or no results filter interaction
Filter values wrong (timezone on dates, tenant ID format) a data problem, not the index

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Prove it — 500 tenants in one index, post-filter the top-100:

import random
random.seed(0)
tenants = [random.randrange(500) for _ in range(100_000)]          # 500 tenants, shared index
hits = sorted(range(100_000), key=lambda i: random.random())[:100]  # ANN returns top-100 regardless of tenant
mine = [i for i in hits if tenants[i] == 42]                         # post-filter to tenant 42
print(len(hits), len(mine))
# → 100 0

A tenant with 0.2% of the data expects ~0.2 results out of 100 after post-filtering — here, none.

stages.name: Fix by design
stages.claim: filter inside the search, or partition by tenant
stages.html:
Approach How Trade-off
filtered ANN filter during traversal; exact search fallback when selective engine-dependent; benchmark it
partition per tenant namespace / shard / collection per tenant many small indexes; memory and ops overhead
hybrid partitioning dedicated for large tenants, shared + filtered for the tail two paths to operate
time partitions index per month/quarter date filter becomes partition choice

stages.name: Validate
stages.html: • Benchmark recall@10 and p95 per tenant size class (largest, median, smallest) with real date ranges; CI canary that a tenant never retrieves another tenant's chunks.

followUps.question: 🧪 A tenant owns 30% of the corpus. Does post-filtering still work?
followUps.html:
Mostly.

top 100 × 30% of the corpus ≈ 30 survivors      ← may be enough

The problem is worst for small tenants and narrow date ranges. Results differ by tenant size, so benchmark per size class.

followUps.question: "Just increase k to 10,000 and filter afterwards."
followUps.html:
That hides the design problem.

k = 10,000, then filter
Latency and memory grow a lot
Small tenants may still get nothing

followUps.question: Why does pre-filtering hurt HNSW?
followUps.html:
Because search moves through neighbours, and most of them are now excluded.

Failure:neighbours filtered outpaths disconnectgreedy search gets stuck or needs many more steps

Engines mitigate with filter-aware traversal or a brute-force fallback.

followUps.question: Where do tenant IDs come from?
followUps.html:
From the authenticated principal in the request context.

Source Trusted?
Authenticated principal
The user's text
The LLM

The retrieval service enforces it (Q35).

followUps.question: 10,000 tenants, most tiny. Which design?
followUps.html:
A hybrid, by tenant class.

Tenants Design
The long tail of tiny ones shared index with filtered ANN, or tenant-grouped shards
The few large or regulated ones dedicated partitions

Benchmark per class and monitor per-tenant recall.

dontSay: One benchmark number for all tenant sizes.

rag-q29.testing: separating content churn from model/chunker changes, and a freshness SLA.
rag-q29.trap: swapping the embedding model with no re-index plan.
rag-q29.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "There are two different problems here, and they need different machinery."
2 · Constraints and numbers "Content churn — documents added, edited and deleted all day — is incremental. Changes arrive as events from the source systems: webhooks, change-data-capture, or polling with modification times. For each changed document, I re-parse and re-chunk it, compute a content hash per chunk, re-embed only chunks whose hash changed, and upsert by a stable chunk ID. Deleted documents produce tombstones that remove all their chunks. Permissions changes must propagate the same way. Because graph indexes keep soft-deleted nodes, I schedule compaction."
4 · Deep-dive "Pipeline changes — a new embedding model, a new chunker — invalidate every vector at once. That's not an upsert; it's a blue-green re-index: build a new index in parallel, shadow-query it, compare on the golden set, cut over, and keep the old one for rollback."
6 · What I'd monitor "Freshness gets its own SLA — say, 95 percent of edits searchable within five minutes — and I monitor ingestion lag against it, plus a reconciliation job that compares the source and the index for drift: missing, extra or stale documents."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: what changes, how fast, and what's the SLA?
stages.html: • Edit rate, delete rate, permission changes; sources' change feeds; acceptable staleness.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Prove it — daily churn cost (illustrative):

Corpus: 5M chunks · 2% of documents edited daily
Naive: re-embed every chunk of edited docs        → ~100k embeddings/day
Hash-based: re-embed only changed chunks (~20%)   → ~20k embeddings/day
Full re-index for a model change                  → 5M embeddings (hours, planned)

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
Changes:source systemschange queueworker: parse, chunk, hashembedupsert by chunk ID + version
Deletes:workertombstone deleteindexscheduled compaction
Safety net:reconciler compares source with indexback onto the change queue

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.claim: model and chunker changes are migrations
stages.html:
• Blue/green: new index built from the source, shadow traffic, golden-set diff, cut-over, rollback window (Q31).
  • Never mix embedding versions in one index; stamp every vector with its contract version.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: missed deletes and lagging permissions leak
stages.html:
Failure Effect
missed delete removed content keeps being cited (compliance risk)
permission change lag users see content they lost access to
no hash → full re-embeds cost spikes
stale versions kept contradictory chunks (Q34)
soft deletes piling up recall and memory degrade

stages.name: What I'd monitor
stages.claim: ingestion lag against the freshness SLA
stages.html: • Ingestion lag p95 vs SLA, queue depth, failed documents, reconciliation diffs, index size vs source size, tombstone ratio.

followUps.question: 🧪 A document is edited: one paragraph changed out of 40 chunks. What gets re-embedded?
followUps.html:
Only the chunks whose content hash changed.

  • Usually: one or two chunks.
  • Plus: neighbours, if chunk boundaries shifted.
  • Why it stays cheap: structure-aware chunking keeps boundaries stable.

followUps.question: "Re-index nightly."
followUps.html:
That means up to 24 hours of stale answers.

Nightly re-index Event-driven upserts
Freshness up to 24 hours stale minutes
Deleted content still served until the next run removed
Cost a full re-embed every night only what changed

followUps.question: How do you handle deletes in HNSW?
followUps.html:
Mark now, compact later.

Lifecycle:mark deleted (filtered from results)track the tombstone ratiocompact or rebuild when it's high

followUps.question: How do you know the index matches the source?
followUps.html:
With a reconciliation job.

Job:read document IDs and content hashes from source and indexcomparere-queue the differences

followUps.question: Legal requires deletion within 24 hours. Design for it.
followUps.html:
Delete is its own fast path, with proof.

Path:delete event, processed with prioritytombstone removes chunks from results immediatelycaches invalidatedcompaction removes them physicallyaudit log proves completion

Semantic caches must be keyed so deleted content can't be served.

dontSay: Treating a model swap as an upsert.

rag-q30.testing: per-stage measurement first, and knowing generation usually dominates.
rag-q30.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "First I'd get per-stage spans for slow requests: query rewrite, embedding, vector search, rerank, prompt assembly, time to first token, and total generation. Without that breakdown, any fix is a guess."
2 · Rule out the fakes "In most RAG systems generation dominates: the prompt prefill and then decoding the answer take seconds, while retrieval takes tens to a few hundred milliseconds. If that's the case, optimising the vector index moves nothing."
3 · Confirm with evidence "For generation-bound latency: stream the answer, because users feel time to first token, not total time; send fewer chunks — a reranker lets me go from fifteen chunks to five, which shortens prefill; cap the answer length; cache the stable part of the prompt with provider prompt caching; and route easy questions to a smaller, faster model."
4 · Fix by stage "For retrieval-bound latency: lower efSearch within the recall target, rerank fewer candidates, cache query embeddings and results, and look at the filter — slow filtered search is a common hidden cost. An LLM query-rewrite step before retrieval is also often a surprisingly large chunk, so I only rewrite when needed."
5 · Validate "And a semantic answer cache for repeated questions skips everything, where it's safe."

stages.name: Name it
stages.claim: a tail-latency problem in one stage
stages.html: "Find the stage that owns the p95 before changing anything."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.claim: provider retries and cold starts look alike
stages.html:
Looks like Really is Check
Slow generation provider-side rate limits and retries retry counts
Slow everything cold starts and connection setup first-request vs warm latency
Slow answer the client waiting for the full answer before rendering TTFT may already be fine

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Prove it — a slow request's trace (illustrative):

Span p95 ms
query rewrite (LLM) 450
embed query 25
vector search (filtered) 180
rerank 100 candidates 320
assemble prompt (15 chunks, 6k tokens) 10
TTFT 1,300
generate 400 tokens 1,700
total ~4,000

stages.name: Fix by stage
stages.html:
Stage Levers
generation stream; 15 → 5 chunks; cap output; prompt caching; smaller model on easy routes
rewrite only for conversational/vague queries; smaller model
rerank 100 → 30 candidates (if recall holds); batch on GPU
search efSearch tuned to recall target; filter-aware index; caching
whole pipeline semantic answer cache for repeated questions (tenant- and version-keyed)

stages.name: Validate
stages.html: • Re-measure p95 per stage and end to end; check quality on the golden set didn't drop (fewer chunks, smaller model).

followUps.question: 🧪 You cut vector search from 180 ms to 60 ms. What happens to p95 in the trace above?
followUps.html:
About 4.0 s → 3.9 s: a 3% improvement.

saved: 180 ms − 60 ms = 120 ms of a 4,000 ms p95 ≈ 3%

Generation dominates. That's why you measure first.

followUps.question: "Switch to a faster vector database."
followUps.html:
Only if search owns the latency.

Stage Share in most traces
Vector search a small slice
Context size, streaming, model choice where the win is

followUps.question: Why does sending fewer chunks help so much?
followUps.html:
Because prefill time grows with prompt length.

Chain:fewer, better chunksshorter promptshorter TTFToften a shorter and better answer

Output length tends to grow with context too.

followUps.question: How does streaming change perceived latency?
followUps.html:
Users see text after TTFT, not after the full generation.

Without streaming With streaming
Total time the same the same
First text seen at the end at TTFT

Track TTFT as its own SLO.

followUps.question: What would you put in the SLO?
followUps.html:
Two user-facing numbers, plus stage budgets.

SLO Example
TTFT p95 < 1.5 s
Total p95 per route
Stage-level budgets alert on the stage that breaches, with trace exemplars attached

dontSay: One end-to-end number with no spans.

rag-q31.testing: that vectors across models are incomparable, and a blue/green migration with evidence and rollback.
rag-q31.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "Every existing vector becomes incomparable the moment the model changes: vectors from two models live in different spaces, so a query embedded with the new model can't be compared with documents embedded by the old one. There's no partial migration and no mixed index."
3 · Baseline plan "So it's a blue-green migration. First, justify it: run the new model on the golden set against the current one and confirm the recall gain is real. Then build a second index in parallel by re-embedding the full corpus from the source — not from old vectors — while the old index keeps serving, and keep it in sync by dual-writing new changes to both. Shadow a slice of live queries against the new index and compare results and metrics. Cut over, ideally gradually, keeping the old index for a rollback window, then retire it."
4 · Deep-dive "Along the way: a dimension change means re-planning memory and index parameters; the reranker and chunk size may need retuning; and every vector and query carries a version stamp so a query never searches an index embedded with a different model."
Close "Budget the re-embedding cost and time — it's the full corpus."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: why upgrade, and what else changes?
stages.html: • Quality gain measured? Vendor deprecation? Dimension, max length, prefixes, languages?

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
Prove it — full re-embed of 8M chunks (illustrative):

8M chunks × 350 tokens = 2.8B tokens to embed
Self-hosted at ~5,000 chunks/s per GPU  → ~27 min per GPU-pass (plus I/O)
API at a rate limit of 1M tokens/min    → ~47 hours — plan throughput and cost first
Dimension 768 → 1,024: vector memory +33%

stages.name: Baseline plan
Deep-dive
stages.html:
Component Check after the swap
chunk size vs new max length truncation?
query/document prefixes new conventions applied?
reranker candidate count recall plateau moved?
semantic cache invalidate (keys include embedding version)
similarity thresholds re-calibrate — scores shift with the model

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: mixed vector spaces and stale thresholds
stages.html: • Mixed-version index; queries embedded with the new model against old vectors; thresholds silently wrong; cache serving old answers; no rollback path.

stages.name: What I'd monitor
stages.html: • Shadow comparison metrics, answer groundedness and abstention rate before/after, retrieval-score distribution shift, dual-write lag.

followUps.question: 🧪 After cut-over, abstention jumps from 4% to 19%. First suspect?
followUps.html:
A similarity or rerank threshold calibrated for the old model.

Why:the new model's cosine scores sit in a different rangemore results fall below the cut-offmore abstentions

Re-calibrate thresholds on the golden set.

followUps.question: "Re-embed in place, it's just an update."
followUps.html:
No: mid-update, the index mixes two vector spaces.

In place Parallel build, then cut over
During the update results are garbage old index serves
Rollback none switch back

followUps.question: Why re-embed from the source rather than old chunks?
followUps.html:
Because the source is the authority.

  • Old chunks may be stale or missing recent edits.
  • The migration is the chance to apply the new model's optimal chunking and prefixes.

followUps.question: Can you avoid a full re-embed?
followUps.html:
Not if vectors must be comparable.

Avoidable?
Re-embedding no, for production quality; embedding-space adapters are research
Re-parsing yes: store the parsed chunks

followUps.question: The API vendor deprecates your embedding model in 90 days. Plan?
followUps.html:
Start now, and use it to reduce future exposure.

Plan:evaluate candidates on the golden setpick oneschedule the re-embed within rate limits and budgetblue/green with shadowingcut over

Consider a self-hosted model to control future deprecations.

rag-q32.testing: splitting cost into buckets, knowing generation usually dominates, and the right levers.
rag-q32.trap: optimising vector storage while generation is most of the spend.
rag-q32.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "I'd split spend into four buckets before touching anything. Embedding: a one-off cost at ingestion plus churn — usually small. Storage and memory for the index: always on, grows with the corpus and dimension. Reranking: per query, GPU or API. And generation: per query, input tokens for the prompt and retrieved chunks, plus output tokens — in most systems this is the biggest bucket by far."
2 · Rule out the fakes "Then I check for the fakes that inflate the bill: retries after timeouts doubling calls, a retrieval loop or agent running more steps than expected, full re-embeds triggered by a pipeline bug, or one tenant with abusive volume."
4 · Fix by bucket "Levers, largest first for a generation-dominated bill: send fewer chunks by reranking; use provider prompt caching on the stable prefix — system prompt and instructions; route easy queries to a smaller model; cap output length; and a semantic answer cache for repeated questions, keyed by tenant and content version. For the storage bucket: int8 or binary quantisation and Matryoshka truncation shrink always-on memory a lot. For embedding: re-embed only changed chunks."
5 · Validate "And I'd attribute cost per tenant and per feature so the next increase is visible the day it starts."

stages.html:
Bucket Driver Typical share
generation (prompt + chunk + output tokens) × queries usually largest
rerank candidates × queries moderate
storage / RAM vectors × dims × bytes, always on grows with corpus
embedding ingest + churn small unless re-embeds loop

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html: • Retry storms, runaway agent loops, re-embed bugs, cache misses from bad keys, one noisy tenant.

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.html:
Prove it — cost model (illustrative unit prices, not quotes):

Queries: 3M/month
Generation input:  (800 prompt + 12 chunks × 400) = 5,600 tokens × 3M = 16.8B tokens
Generation output: 350 tokens × 3M = 1.05B tokens
Rerank: 100 candidates × 3M = 300M pairs
Storage: 10M chunks × 1,024 dims × 4 B = 41 GB RAM, always on
→ even at modest per-token prices, the 16.8B input tokens dominate
After: rerank 100 → 30, send 4 chunks → 2,400 input tokens (−57%); cache the 800-token prefix

stages.name: Fix by bucket
stages.claim: a lever per bucket, biggest bucket first
stages.html:
Bucket Levers
generation fewer chunks, prompt caching, smaller model on easy routes, output caps, answer cache
rerank fewer candidates, smaller reranker, skip for lookups
storage int8/binary + rescoring, Matryoshka truncation, tiered storage
embedding hash-based incremental re-embeds

stages.name: Validate
stages.claim: cost per query with quality unchanged
stages.html: • Cost per query and per tenant before/after, with golden-set quality unchanged.

followUps.question: 🧪 Dropping from 12 to 4 chunks of 400 tokens with an 800-token prompt: input tokens per query go from? to?

5,600 → 2,400 tokens: a 57% cut.

before: 12 × 400 + 800 = 5,600 input tokens
after:   4 × 400 + 800 = 2,400 input tokens

followUps.question: "Move to a cheaper vector database."

Worth checking, but storage is a small share of most RAG bills.

Order:find the dominant bucketthen cut it

followUps.question: How does prompt caching help RAG?
followUps.html:
It discounts the stable prefix, not the chunks.

Part of the prompt Cached?
System prompt, instructions, examples yes: billed at a reduced rate on repeat calls
Retrieved chunks rarely: they change per query

So put the stable part first and the chunks after it.

With care.

Rule

Threshold a high similarity
Invalidate on document changes
Never cache personalised answers

followUps.question: How do you stop the next surprise bill?
followUps.html:
Make cost visible before it's spent.

Control

Budgets with alerts
Rate limits in tokens
Design review a cost line for every new feature

rag-q33.testing: the position effect, and that fewer, better-placed chunks beat more.
rag-q33.trap: responding to bad answers by raising k.
rag-q33.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Plain definition "Lost in the middle is the finding, from Liu and colleagues in 2023, that language models use information at the start and end of a long context much better than information in the middle. In their multi-document question-answering experiments, accuracy followed a U-shape: highest when the relevant document was first or last, lowest when it sat in the middle, and sometimes worse than having no documents at all. Newer models have improved, but position effects haven't disappeared, and they grow with context length."
2 · Mechanism "For RAG it means that retrieving more chunks isn't free: every extra chunk pushes others toward the middle and dilutes attention."
3 · Where it bites "What I do: send fewer, higher-precision chunks — that's the reranker's main job. Order them deliberately: the best chunks at the start and end of the context block, weaker ones in the middle. Remove duplicates and near-duplicates. Compress or filter chunks to the relevant sentences when they're long. And restate the question after the context, so the instruction sits at the end. Then I verify on the golden set by placing the gold chunk at different positions and checking answer accuracy — that tells me how much my model and prompt actually suffer from it."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Information at the edges of the context is used best; information in the middle is used worst." (Liu et al., 2023)

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
• Instructions tend to be at the start and questions at the end in training data; attention concentrates on early tokens and recent tokens.
  • More context means more competition for the model's attention.

stages.name: Where it bites
What I do
stages.html:
Prove it — reorder so the best chunks sit at the edges:

ranked = ["c1", "c2", "c3", "c4", "c5", "c6"]    # best first, from the reranker
front, back = ranked[0::2], ranked[1::2]
print(front + back[::-1])
# → ['c1', 'c3', 'c5', 'c6', 'c4', 'c2']

The top two chunks end up first and last; the weakest sit in the middle.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Budget evidence tokens explicitly and measure accuracy vs number of chunks; the curve often peaks early.

followUps.question: 🧪 Answers are wrong; the gold chunk is 9th of 15 in the prompt. What do you change first?
followUps.html:
Rerank and send 4–5 chunks, with the gold-like chunks at the edges.

Move Effect
Rerank, send fewer the gold chunk leaves the middle
Raise k pushes it further into the middle: don't

followUps.question: "Newer models fixed lost in the middle."
followUps.html:
Improved, not eliminated.

  • It depends on the task and the length.
  • Test your model: move the gold chunk around and measure.

followUps.question: Does the effect exist for short contexts?
followUps.html:
Much less.

Context Position effect
3–5 short chunks matters little
Longer context, more documents grows

followUps.question: What's context compression?
followUps.html:
Sending only the relevant sentences of each chunk.

Path:retrieved chunksmall model or extractive methodrelevant sentences onlyprompt
  • Gain: fewer tokens, less noise.
  • Risk: dropping context the answer needed.

followUps.question: How would you measure it in your system?
followUps.html:
By moving the gold chunk and measuring.

Test:golden questionsgold chunk at position 1, middle and last among distractorsaccuracy per position, for your model and prompt

Use the result to set k and the ordering.

rag-q34.testing: that conflicts are a data problem first, fixed with metadata, and surfaced rather than averaged.
rag-q34.trap: calling it hallucination and tightening the prompt.
rag-q34.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Name it "Usually the model silently picks one — often the one that appears first, or the one closer to its own prior belief — and states it confidently. It looks like a hallucination, but it's a different failure: the evidence itself disagreed."
2 · Rule out the fakes "The most common cause is versions: the 2024 and 2025 policies both indexed, or a draft and a final. Other causes are genuinely different scopes — EU versus US terms — and sources of different authority, like an official policy versus a forum post."
4 · Fix with metadata and policy "So the fixes are mostly metadata, not prompting. At ingestion, supersede old versions instead of accumulating them, and attach effective dates, version, region and source authority to every chunk. At retrieval, filter to current and applicable versions, and prefer authoritative sources. At generation, when a real conflict remains, instruct the model to surface it — 'the 2025 policy says 30 days; an older FAQ says 14' — with citations, or to ask which scope applies, rather than choosing silently or averaging."
5 · Validate "And I'd monitor it: a conflict check on retrieved sets, and alerts when two versions of the same document are retrieved together."

stages.name: Name it
stages.html: "The model resolves a conflict silently; the fix is to prevent, filter or surface the conflict."

stages.name: Rule out the fakes
stages.html:
Cause Fix
stale + current version supersede at ingestion; filter by effective date
different scopes (region, plan) scope metadata; ask or filter by user context
authority mismatch source-rank metadata; prefer official
true disagreement surface both with citations

stages.name: Confirm with evidence
stages.claim: the stale chunk is visible in the trace
stages.html:
Prove it — a metadata filter that removes the stale chunk:

chunks = [
    {"id": "pol-2024#3", "doc": "refund-policy", "effective": "2024-01-01", "text": "Refunds within 14 days."},
    {"id": "pol-2025#3", "doc": "refund-policy", "effective": "2025-03-01", "text": "Refunds within 30 days."},
]
latest = {}
for c in chunks:
    if c["doc"] not in latest or c["effective"] > latest[c["doc"]]["effective"]: latest[c["doc"]] = c
print([c["id"] for c in latest.values()])
# → ['pol-2025#3']

stages.name: Fix with metadata and policy
stages.html:
Stage Control
Ingestion version and supersede; effective dates; scope; authority
Retrieval filter to current and applicable; rank by authority
Generation "If sources conflict, state both with citations and say which applies, or ask."

stages.name: Validate
stages.html: • Golden questions with known conflicts; check the answer cites the current source or surfaces the conflict.

followUps.question: 🧪 Both "Refunds within 14 days" (2024) and "30 days" (2025) are in the prompt, 2024 first. Likely answer without guidance?
followUps.html:
A confident single answer, plausibly "14 days", which is wrong.

Setup Likely answer
No guidance the first or more familiar value: 14 days
Date metadata shown, plus a conflict instruction 30 days (effective March 2025), citing the newer policy

followUps.question: "Tell the model to always pick the newest."
followUps.html:
That's a backstop, not the fix.

"Pick the newest"
Works only if dates are in the context and reliable
Breaks for scope differences

Fix it in metadata and filters; keep the prompt as the backstop.

followUps.question: Should you keep old versions at all?
followUps.html:
Yes, for historical questions, but out of default retrieval.

Query Old versions
Default marked superseded and excluded
Asks about the past ("what was the policy in 2024?") included

followUps.question: How do you detect conflicts automatically?
followUps.html:
Two checks on the retrieved set.

Check Catches
Chunks from different versions of the same document version conflicts
An NLI or LLM contradiction check between top chunks (optional) content conflicts

followUps.question: Who owns the metadata?
followUps.html:
Content owners and the ingestion pipeline together.

Owner Provides
Source systems effective dates and status
Governance step fills in where the source doesn't

RAG quality is partly a content-management problem.

spine: Why the model can't be the control
Residual risk and what I monitor
rag-q35.testing: an explicit isolation model, principal-derived filters inside retrieval, ACL freshness, and tests.
rag-q35.trap: post-retrieval filtering — that's a data leak.
rag-q35.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The asset and the attacker "I'd state the isolation model first, because everything follows from it. Three options. An index per tenant gives the strongest isolation and simple deletion, but it gets expensive past hundreds of tenants. A shared index with a tenant filter scales to thousands, but correctness then depends entirely on the filter. A hybrid gives large or regulated tenants dedicated indexes and puts the long tail in a shared one."
2 · The leak paths "In the shared case, the filter must come from the authenticated principal in the request context — never from the user's text, and never from anything the LLM produces. It's applied inside the vector search, as part of the query, not as a post-filter on results, and the retrieval service enforces it so no caller can forget it."
3 · Why the model can't be the control "Tenant isolation is only half; document-level permissions inside a tenant are the harder half, because permissions change after indexing. Either re-check access against the source of truth at retrieval time, or copy ACLs into the index and commit to a maximum staleness window with monitoring."
4 · Layered controls "Then everything around retrieval must be tenant-scoped too: caches keyed by tenant, logs and traces redacted, evaluation sets separated, and no shared fine-tuned model trained on multiple tenants' data."
5 · Residual risk and what I monitor "Finally, test it: a CI canary that queries as tenant A with content only tenant B has and asserts zero results, plus audit logs of which chunks were served to whom."

stages.name: The asset and the attacker
stages.html:
• Asset: every tenant's documents and derived data (chunks, embeddings, cached answers).
  • Attacker: a legitimate user of another tenant, a user within a tenant lacking document permission, or injected content steering tool use.

stages.name: The leak paths
stages.claim: filters, caches, logs and fine-tunes can all leak
stages.html:
Path Example
retrieval filter missing/wrong tenant ID taken from request body
post-filtering cross-tenant chunks enter memory, logs or the prompt before filtering
stale ACLs a user removed from a folder still retrieves it
shared caches semantic cache returns another tenant's answer
logs / traces chunk text in shared observability tools
shared fine-tunes model memorises one tenant's data

stages.name: Why the model can't be the control
stages.claim: an instruction is not an access control
stages.html: • "Only use documents for tenant X" in the prompt is an instruction, not an access control; if forbidden chunks reach the prompt, the leak has happened.

stages.name: Layered controls
stages.claim: principal-derived filter inside retrieval, plus canaries
stages.html:
Prove it — the CI canary:

def test_no_cross_tenant_retrieval(search):
    marker = "CANARY-7f3a tenant-B-only phrase"
    results = search(query=marker, principal={"tenant": "A", "groups": ["all"]})
    assert all(r.tenant == "A" for r in results)
    assert not any(marker in r.text for r in results)

stages.name: Residual risk and what I monitor
stages.claim: ACL lag and filter bugs, watched per deploy
stages.html:
• ACL staleness window; bugs in filter construction; operator access.
  • Monitor: canary results per deploy, audit logs of served chunk IDs vs principal, ACL sync lag, cache key audits.

followUps.question: The API takes tenant_id from the JSON body. What's the attack?
followUps.html:
Any authenticated user sends another tenant's ID and reads their documents.

Tenant ID from Safe?
The JSON body
The verified token or session, server-side

followUps.question: "We filter results by tenant before showing them."
followUps.html:
Too late: the forbidden chunks were already fetched.

A fetched chunk can leak into
The prompt
Logs
Caches

Small tenants also get starved results. Filter inside retrieval.

followUps.question: Index per tenant or shared?
followUps.html:
It depends on tenant count and size.

Design Fits
Index per tenant moderate tenant counts: strong isolation, easy deletion, noisy-neighbour control
Shared + filtered thousands of small tenants
Hybrid mixed sizes (Q28)

followUps.question: How do you delete a tenant?
followUps.html:
Easy with an index per tenant; a procedure with a shared one.

Design Deletion
Per-tenant index drop it
Shared index delete by tenant filter → compact → purge caches → backups per retention policy

Either way, prove completion in an audit log.

followUps.question: A regulated customer asks for proof of isolation. What do you show?
followUps.html:
Five pieces of evidence, and an option.

Evidence
The isolation model, and where the filter is enforced
Canary test results in CI
Audit logs of served chunks
ACL sync SLAs

Optionally, a dedicated index or deployment for them.

rag-q36.testing: two evaluation problems, a golden set, calibrated judges, and cheap leading indicators for alerts.
rag-q36.trap: end-to-end evaluation only — it can't tell you where it broke.
rag-q36.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "RAG evaluation is two problems. Retrieval: did we find the evidence? That's classic information retrieval — recall@k, MRR, nDCG — against labelled relevant chunks. Generation: given the evidence, is the answer good? That's the RAG triad — context relevance, groundedness or faithfulness, and answer relevance — usually scored by an LLM judge, plus correctness against reference answers where we have them."
2 · The golden set "Everything starts with a golden set: questions with their answering chunks and reference answers. I bootstrap it by generating questions from chunks with an LLM, then humans curate it and add real questions from logs, especially failures, stratified by query type. Without it, every discussion is opinion. Offline, the golden set gates CI: every change to chunking, embeddings, prompts or models runs component metrics and end-to-end metrics, and regressions block the release. The judge is calibrated against human labels and its model version is pinned like any dependency."
6 · What I'd page on "Online, I don't page on judge scores — they're expensive, noisy and lagging. I page on cheap leading indicators: abstention rate, the distribution of top retrieval scores, empty-result rate, ingestion lag against the freshness SLA, latency and error rates per stage."
Close "Judge scores on sampled traffic and user feedback go to dashboards and weekly review, and failing traces flow back into the golden set."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
Problem Metrics Needs
retrieval recall@k, precision@k, MRR, nDCG, hit rate relevant-chunk labels
generation context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance, correctness judge (calibrated) or references

stages.name: The golden set
stages.html: • Synthetic Q&A per chunk → human curation → add real queries and failures → stratify (lookup, multi-hop, aggregation, unanswerable) → version it (Q61).

stages.name: Offline evaluation
stages.html:
Prove it — the release gate (cells to measure, thresholds illustrative):

Metric Baseline Candidate Gate
recall@20 measure measure no drop > 2 pts
groundedness measure measure no drop > 2 pts
answer correctness measure measure ≥ baseline − CI
abstention on unanswerable measure measure ≥ 90%
p95 latency, cost/query measure measure within budget

stages.name: Online signals
stages.html:
Signal Why it leads
abstention rate spikes when retrieval or ingestion breaks
top-1 retrieval score distribution shifts on drift or broken embeddings
empty-result rate per tenant filter or ACL bugs
ingestion lag freshness SLA
thumbs-down / regenerate rate user-visible quality

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: stale sets, uncalibrated judges, one score
stages.html: • Golden set drifts from real traffic; uncalibrated judge; single end-to-end score; paging on noisy judge metrics; no slice analysis.

stages.name: What I'd page on
stages.html:
• Page: abstention or empty-result spikes, score-distribution shift, ingestion lag breach, stage error/latency SLO breaches.
  • Dashboard + weekly review: sampled judge scores, feedback, golden-set re-runs.

followUps.question: 🧪 Abstention jumps from 5% to 25% overnight with no deploy. Likely causes?
followUps.html:
Something upstream changed.

Suspect Check
Ingestion broke (new documents missing, parser failure) ingestion lag
An ACL or filter change emptied results empty-result rate by tenant
The embedding API changed or failed score distributions
A new query pattern arrived query logs

followUps.question: "We evaluate end to end with an LLM judge, that's enough."
followUps.html:
It tells you quality dropped, not where.

Metric Answers
End-to-end judge did quality drop?
Component metrics (recall@k, groundedness) at which stage?

And the judge itself needs calibration.

followUps.question: How big should the golden set be?
followUps.html:
Large enough to detect the differences you care about, per slice.

  • Typical size: a few hundred to a few thousand questions.
  • Per slice: enough for each important one (language, query type, tenant class).

followUps.question: Reference-free vs reference-based metrics?
followUps.html:
Use both: reference-based offline, reference-free online.

Reference-free Reference-based
Examples groundedness, context relevance correctness against a gold answer
Needs labels no yes
Strength scales to live traffic more reliable

followUps.question: Who owns the golden set?
followUps.html:
The product team, with domain experts.

  • Versioned like code.
  • Refreshed from production failures monthly.
  • Durable: it survives every model and index change, so it's the longest-lived asset in the system.
